title: Ghadir Khumm
hook: both traditions report the Prophet ﷺ saying, of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla, and they read it differently

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shia telling, and the word imam. Your line was designated, they say.

A watering place on the road between Mecca and Medina, called Khumm. Tradition knows the spot as Ghadir Khumm, the pool of Khumm. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops there with the people traveling with him, and stands up to speak. Sahih Muslim records the scene through the companion Zayd ibn Arqam. The Prophet says he is only a human being, and that the messenger of his Lord will soon come for him. He is speaking like someone saying goodbye. Today: Ghadir Khumm.
screen: `A POOL ON THE ROAD.` → `HE STANDS TO SPEAK.` → `LIKE SOMEONE SAYING GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: In Muslim's report, the Prophet goes on: I am leaving among you two weighty things. The first is the Book of God, in which is guidance and light, so hold fast to it. The second is the people of my house. And he says, more than once: I remind you of God concerning the people of my house. Then the line at the center of today. Al-Tirmidhi records it: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. Sunni and Shia collections both carry these words, and both communities honor them. They read them differently because of one word. Mawla carries more than one meaning. A few days ago it described Salim, the freed man linked to Abu Hudhayfah's house. Readers of this hadith have heard in it friend, ally, protector, patron, or master. In the Sunni reading, it means love and loyalty here: whoever takes me as his friend should love and stand by Ali. Some of them connect it to a tension reported in Bukhari: Buraydah, who had been with Ali on a mission, resented him, and the Prophet told him not to hate Ali. In this reading, Ghadir is a public defense of Ali and a call to love him. Shia Muslims read mawla here as master, the one with authority over the believers. In their reading, the Prophet is naming his successor in front of the people, by God's command, and the words about his household point the same way. Shia communities mark the day as a festival, Eid al-Ghadir. Same pool, same sentence: two readings, held with deep conviction, each with its scholars and its reasons.
screen: `TWO WEIGHTY THINGS.` · `OF WHOMEVER I AM HIS MAWLA.` · `FRIEND AND ALLY, SOME READ.` · `MASTER AND LEADER, OTHERS READ.` · then, large: `THE SAME WORDS, TWO READINGS.`

segments.voice: Say the line to yourself slowly: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. On one breath, hear it the first way: friend, ally, someone to love and stand beside. On the next, hear it the second way: master, leader, the one appointed to guide. Don't choose; just notice how much one word can carry.
Ghadir Khumm. The pool of Khumm, between Mecca and Medina, where the Prophet spoke of the Book and his household, and said of Ali: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. Today's word.
Your line: the same words, two readings. One sentence, honored by both. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims both narrate the hadith of Ghadir Khumm; Shia Muslims celebrate Eid al-Ghadir as the day the Prophet designated Ali, while Sunni scholars teach it as a call to love and support Ali.

chat.says: What did the Prophet say at Ghadir Khumm, and why do Muslims read it differently?
options: Of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla; and mawla can mean friend or master.
He announced the date of his death, so people could prepare to mourn.
He only told the travelers how long to rest at the pool before Medina.
chat.meaning: Sunni and Shia collections both carry the line. Mawla can mean friend, ally or master, and the two traditions read it differently.

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory: confirm Muslim 2408, Tirmidhi 3713 (narrator given as Zayd ibn Arqam; Tirmidhi's chain may differ, please confirm), Bukhari 4350.
The gloss of ghadir as a pool and the range of meanings for mawla are lexical claims not stated in the cited hadith; a Keeper should confirm them against a standard lexicon (Lane) or cut.
The hook places the stop on the road between Mecca and Medina as Muslim's report does; the return from the Farewell Pilgrimage and the date are not stated in the script.
Fork 'answer' is the third option ('both readings have their scholars') to avoid the app crediting one tradition's reading as correct. Confirm.
Sunni reading linked to the Yemen complaint (Bukhari 4350) is one Sunni explanation among others; worded as 'some of them'. Both Keepers should read 864–866 together for balance.
